newsitem.title: UK: No clear winner seen emerging in "green" car race.
newsitem.headline: No clear winner seen emerging in "green" car race.

text.p: As the world's industrialised nations argue over scaling back polluting carbon emissions, carmakers are jostling to develop the definitive "green" car.

But the contest between fuel cell motors, electric cars, gas-powered vehicles and assorted hybrids is not likely to lead to total dominance of one technology at the expense of the competition, industry sources said.
"Fuels will be chosen to suit particular situations," said Jonathan Murray, manager of transport projects for the Energy Saving Trust in the U.K.
"The car market is already fragmented," he said. "We are going to see the same thing in the alternative fuels market."
Developers of cleaner technologies are quick to tout their own systems as "the answer" to pollution.
Dietmar Fritsche, spokesman for German car makers Volkswagen AG, said hybrid petrol/electric technology leads the pack.
Toyota Motor Corp also said on Monday it would be making 1,000 new petrol/electric hybrid cars per month and the first of these would hit the roads by the end of this year.
Running at 80 miles per gallon, the car cuts carbon emissions by half - but costs $4,000 more than its petrol equivalent.
British firm XKF Developments is also seeking to store energy in spinning "fly wheels" to build what it calls a "Power Beam" hybrid, which could more than double a car's efficiency.

But David Woods, a senior lecturer in engineering at Durham University, sees pure electric car technology as the easiest way to move pollution away from smoky town centres towards power stations -- where emissions can be far more easily managed.
"A hybrid is immediately more expensive because it has two motors," he said. "The answer for now is to have your second car electric, for driving round town. That market is ripe."

The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) tipped fuel cells to become as important a motor for the 21st century as any alternative. These cells belch out nothing more polluting than water, and avoid wasteful combustion processes by using catalysts to convert a hydrogen fuel directly into electricity.
Shares soared by a quarter this month in Ballard Power Systems Inc of Canada, which is developing fuel cells, after Daimler-Benz AG decided to buy a 25 percent stake in the company.
"(Ballard) is not just a concept stock any more," one analyst said. "It is a money-generating proposition."

But the EIU said in a report that conventional engines would still be providing 90 percent of the world's power in 15 years' time, and added that they could easily squeeze plenty more miles from a gallon of gasoline.
Volkswagen's Frische said direct-injection petrol engines may, in the future, use just three litres of fuel per 100 kilometres, compared with six litres for many cars on the road today.
"The good old diesel engine and petrol engines still offer so much potential," he said. "Do we need alternatives yet?"
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is another clean fuel which is already used in some four million vehicles world-wide.

Carbon emissions are cut in half, other emissions are slashed to almost zero, and a conventional car can be converted to running on LPG in a few hours at a cost of $1250-$2500, according to Shell Gas, which introduced Britain's first purpose-built LPG bus last week.
"It has the potential to revolutionise the public transport system," said Shell Gas' Managing Director Pascal Rambaud.
And last year the number of vehicles running on compressed natural gas (CNG) passed the million mark world-wide.
Murray said that while electric motors may be best for town buses, LPC or CNG engines would be better in hillier areas. "It is just a question of economics. There won't be a clear winner."
But analysts stress tighter legislation is needed to force unwilling motorists to buy greener cars.

The U.S. -- with just five percent of the world's population accounts for almost a quarter of all the world's greenhouse gas emissions -- foiled an attempt by European countries at the Group of Seven industrialised nations summit in Denver last week to set specific targets for cutting greenhouse gases.
Rambaud said that despite heavy taxation in Europe, the incentives are not enough.
"We will not make massive investments into thousands of forecourts until the fuel is attractive enough."
Some carmakers in the U.S. even appear to be reversing the trend, encouraged by gasoline prices which are just a fraction of those in many other countries.

Ford Motor Co is testing a family car which is so big it is not classified as a light vehicle and thus is exempt from federal taxes aimed at gas-guzzlers. Measuring 19 feet in length, and weighing three tonnes, it would be the largest mass-produced family car ever built.
